title: Ashwagandha tincture for burnout
subtitle: A root tincture for chronic stress and depletion
excerpt: Dried ashwagandha root macerated in 40% vodka for four to six weeks, then strained and bottled. Traditionally used in Ayurvedic practice and now widely adopted in western herbal medicine for chronic stress, burnout, and fatigue from sustained pressure. Two to four ml in water twice daily for a three-month course. Not for use in pregnancy.
sourceNotes: WHO monograph on Withania somnifera (2002) : pharmacology, traditional uses, safety. EMA HMPC monograph on Withania somnifera (2014) : traditional-use assessment, adaptogenic framing. Chopra et al. (2017), Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition : systematic review of ashwagandha on stress and cortisol. Tincture preparation method follows British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983) folk-tincture conventions. Safety flags for thyroid, autoimmune, and Solanaceae allergen drawn from WHO and EMA assessments.

recipe.yieldDescription: About 140 ml tincture (approximately 35 doses at 4 ml each)
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Maceration takes 4 to 6 weeks before straining. The finished tincture keeps 2 years in dark glass.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Store in a cool, dark cupboard in amber glass with a tight-fitting lid or dropper. Discard if the colour or smell changes markedly.

glossaryTerms.definition: A preparation in which plant material is macerated in alcohol (usually 40% spirit) to extract both water-soluble and fat-soluble constituents. The alcohol also acts as a preservative, giving the preparation a shelf life of two years or more.

A term used in herbal medicine for herbs traditionally associated with supporting the body's capacity to cope with sustained stress. The term describes a functional category, not a biochemical mechanism.

projectSchedule.title: Start your tincture
projectSchedule.body: Pack the dried ashwagandha root into a clean maceration jar. Pour over the 40% vodka so the root is fully covered with at least 2 cm of liquid above. Seal tightly, label with today's date, and store in a cool dark cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Check the liquid level
projectSchedule.body: Open the jar and check the vodka still covers the herb. Dried root can absorb liquid as it softens. Top up with a little more 40% vodka if needed so the herb stays submerged. Seal and return to the cupboard.

projectSchedule.title: Taste and check colour
projectSchedule.body: Pour off a few drops into a small spoon. The tincture should taste earthy and slightly bitter, with the distinctive ashwagandha note. The liquid should be a warm amber-brown. Give the jar a gentle shake and return it to the cupboard for another two weeks.

projectSchedule.title: Strain and bottle
projectSchedule.body: Your tincture is ready. Line a sieve with a double layer of muslin over a clean jug and pour the maceration through. Squeeze the spent herb firmly. Funnel the strained tincture into amber dropper bottles. Label with the herb, the spirit percentage, and the strain date.

content.text: Ashwagandha
tincture
is dried ashwagandha root macerated in 40% vodka for four to six weeks, then strained and bottled for use as a daily adaptogenic preparation. Ashwagandha is an
adaptogen

in Ayurvedic tradition and has been adopted into western herbal practice for burnout, chronic stress, and depletion from sustained pressure. It does not produce an immediate, noticeable effect; it works over a course of weeks, supporting the body's capacity to cope with ongoing demands. The ratio here is one part dried root to five parts 40% spirit by weight. The finished
tincture
keeps two years in dark glass.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms. Do not use ashwagandha in pregnancy. Thyroid: ashwagandha may raise thyroid hormone levels. If you take thyroid medication, speak to your prescriber first. Autoimmune conditions: ashwagandha has immune-modulating activity. Readers with lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, or a similar autoimmune condition should consult a herbalist before use. Allergen: ashwagandha is in the Solanaceae family (alongside tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes). Readers with a sensitivity to Solanaceae plants should approach this herb cautiously. Course length: take for three months, then review. Do not use indefinitely without a break.

content.text: Ingredients

items.prepNote: dried root, broken or coarsely ground
plain 40% vodka (the alcohol percentage matters; do not substitute with a lower-strength spirit)

content.text: Method
Step 1: Pack and cover

Put the dried ashwagandha root into a clean soaking period jar. Pour over the vodka. The root must be fully submerged with at least 2 cm of liquid above it. Any root not covered by alcohol can go mouldy. Seal tightly. Label the jar with the herb, the date, and the spirit percentage.
Step 2: Macerate four to six weeks

Store the jar in a cool, dark cupboard. Give it a gentle shake every few days. After two weeks, check the liquid level: dried root absorbs alcohol as it softens and the level may have dropped. Top up with a little more vodka if needed. At four weeks, taste a few drops: the
tincture
should have an earthy, slightly bitter flavour with the distinctive ashwagandha note. Leave for up to six weeks for a more concentrated result.
Step 3: Strain and bottle

Line a sieve or small colander with a double layer of muslin over a clean jug. Pour the soaking period through. Gather the muslin and press the spent root firmly to extract the last of the liquid. Funnel into clean amber dropper bottles. Label with the herb, spirit percentage, and the strain date.
Dosing

Two to four ml (two to four droppers full) in a small glass of water, twice daily. Morning and early afternoon work well for most people. Course length: three months is the standard course. After three months, take a break of at least four weeks before considering another course. If there is no noticeable shift in energy, sleep quality, or stress resilience after six to eight weeks, consult a herbalist for a more tailored assessment.
Storage
Store in amber glass dropper bottles in a cool, dark cupboard. The
tincture

keeps two years from the strain date. The colour may deepen a little over time; this is normal. Discard if the smell changes markedly or if anything unusual grows in the bottle (a sign of contamination from poor technique).
When not to use this remedy

Do not use in pregnancy. Do not use if you are on thyroid hormone replacement without consulting your prescriber first. Do not use if you have an autoimmune condition without consulting a herbalist. See a doctor for fatigue lasting more than a few weeks, fatigue with weight loss, fatigue with shortness of breath, or fatigue that does not improve with rest and sleep. These can indicate conditions that need medical assessment rather than herbal support.
